newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU acts to reassure consumers about food safety.
newsitem.headline: EU acts to reassure consumers about food safety.

text.p: The European Commission announced plans on Wednesday for reforming its approach to food safety in a bid to reassure consumers in the wake of the mad cow disease crisis.
The European Union executive said it would add 263 officials to its new food safety division, reorganise its system for seeking scientific advice and strengthen its inspection procedures.
"Recent experience has clearly demonstrated that food safety is not only of concern to the consumer, but is also at the very root of a proper functioning of the market," it said in a statement.

The shake-up fulfils a pledge by Commission President Jacques Santer in February to the European Parliament, which was conducting an inquiry into the EU's handling of the mad cow crisis that led to a ban on British beef exports.
That promise helped persuade the parliament to delay a possible motion to censure the Commission.
The Commission said its food safety activities would be grouped in a Food and Veterinary Office that will be set up in Ireland, reporting to Consumer Affairs Commissioner Emma Bonino.

It pledged to seek advice on food safety from eminent and fully independent scientists whose opinions and working methods would be accessible to all interested parties. The Commission's various scientific advisory committees would be regrouped and coordinated by a Scientific Steering Committee.

The Commission said it would strengthen food inspection procedures, taking a "plough to plate" approach to ensure the entire food chain is covered. It also promised to introduce formal audit procedures to assess national control scehmes.
It will also ensure that the EU responds quickly to health emergencies and increases consumer information, including through an Internet site.
The new approach takes away powers from Farm Commissioner Franz Fischler and Industry Commissioner Martin Bangemann.
The Commission separately adopted a paper that aims to launch a debate on how the EU should approach food regulation in the future.
It said it was seeking comments on how to meet the expectations of consumers, procuders, manufacturers and traders and on how well its control procedures worked.
